english.html: of Mane, took him for Martin Guerre: of whom nevertheless they had been familiars and intimate friends.

Here is a very strange case: that the most private and particular friends that Martin Guerre had had in his young age should have been placed in such error that they took the said du Tilh for the same Guerre. True it is that the best of it is more astonishing still — to hear that the near kinsfolk, even the four sisters, were in the like error; and more prodigious still, and almost incredible, that the said Bertrande de Rols, wife of the said Martin Guerre, having lived and conversed ten or twelve years with the same Martin Guerre her husband, should have had a like blindfold before her eyes.

Seeing which, and considering that, since the most private and particular friends of the said Martin Guerre were deceived in him, he might well, with some help, deceive and circumvent many others: he resolved to play the tragedy which you have heard above.

It was truly a tragedy for this fine rustic, inasmuch as the issue of it was most deadly and miserable for him. Whereupon, no one is ignorant of the difference between tragedy and comedy. For although both are kinds of fable <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, comedy nevertheless describes and represents, in a low and humble style, the private fortune of men — such as loves, and the ravishing of maidens — so that thereby one may learn what one ought to imitate and follow in this life, and what one ought also to avoid: whence Cicero in some place calls comedy an imitation of life, a mirror of custom, and an image of truth <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>; so named from KOMAI,

notes.original: Ciceron au premier liure des offices.
notes.gloss: The passage where comedy and tragedy are treated together as kinds of poetic fiction was not located; cf. De officiis 1.97–98 on the poets' observance of what is fitting in each character, and 1.104 on the two kinds of jest.

notes.original: Ciceron en l'oraiſon pro Sext. Roſcio.
notes.gloss: The definition of comedy as imitatio vitae, speculum consuetudinis, imago veritatis is transmitted by Donatus (De comoedia 5.1), who attributes it to Cicero; it is not in the extant Pro Sexto Roscio Amerino, whose nearest thought (16.47) is that the poets' fictions show us our own manners in other persons.

re: duquel pourtant ils auoyent eſté fa-
miliers, & intimes amys.
Voici vn cas bien eſtrange, que les plus priuez & pe-
culiers amis qu'euſt eu Martin Guerre, en ſon ieune
aage, fuſſent conſtituez en tel erreur, qu'ils prinſſent le-
dit du Tilh, pour iceluy Guerre: vray que la meilleure
eſt encore plus admirable, d'entendre que les prochains
parẽs, meſmes les quatre ſœurs fuſſent en pareil erreur,
& encor plus prodigieuſe, & preſqu'incroyable, que la-
dite Bertrande de Rols, femme dudict Martin Guerre,
ayant veſcu & conuerſé dix ou douze ans auec iceluy
Martin Guerre ſon mary, euſt vn ſemblable bandeau
deuant ſes yeux.
Quoy voyant & conſiderant, que puis
que les plus priuez, & peculiers amis du-
dit Martin Guerre, eſtoyent deceuz en
luy, il en pourroit bien auec quelque ai-
de deceuoir, & circonuenir beaucoup
d'autres: ſ'aduiſa de iouër la tragedie que
auez ci deuant entendue.
C'eſtoit veritablement tragedie, pour ce gentil ruſtre:
d'autant que l'iſſue en fut fort funeſte, & miſerable,
pour luy. Surquoy nul ne ſçait la differẽce entre trage-
die, & comedie. Car bien que toutes deux ſoyent eſpe-
ces de fable {a}: la comedie pourtant deſcrit & repreſen-
te en ſtile bas, & humble, la fortune priuée des hom-
mes, cõmme des amours, & rauiſſemens de pucelles, à
fin que par là on apprẽne ce qu'on doit imiter & ſuiure
en cette vie, & ce qu'on doit euiter auſſi: dõt Cicerõ en
quelque lieu appelle la comedie, imitatiõ de vie, miroir
de couſtume, & image de verité {b}, ainſi nõmee à KOMAI
